newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel's honesty unquestioned amid Czech squabbling.
newsitem.headline: Havel's honesty unquestioned amid Czech squabbling.

text.p: In a political scene often dominated by squabbling opportunists, President Vaclav Havel stands out as perhaps the only Czech leader whose honesty and decency is acknowledged on all sides.

Havel, who underwent surgery to remove a small malignant tumour from his lung on Monday, has used his unchallenged moral authority to nurture the Czech transformation from the state socialism he overthrew to free market democracy.
But the 60-year-old playwright, a slight man with a nervous smile, has also lamented the dishonesty and corruption which has accompanied the Czech Republic's rush to make money.

"The moral climate in our country must change," Havel said in his latest New Year's address. "All the changes in the political system which we have successfully carried out will be no good if the morals of the jungle prevail among people."
Havel, who led the 1989 "Velvet Revolution" which toppled communism, is one of the few former dissidents still holding high office in the Czech Republic.
He was detained or formally jailed many times after he co-founded Charter 77, eastern Europe's first human rights group, in 1977. He spent five years in prison altogether.
From jail he wrote a series of philosophical letters to his wife, which were later published as "Letters to Olga". Olga Havlova died of cancer in January, aged 62.
Today Czech leaders are now technocrats who found their niche under communism, even if they were not party members.
Rapid privatisation, even when it is is imperfect, has been the watchword of the past five years of government under right-wing Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus.

Few Czech political leaders apart from the non-partisan Havel seem to have stopped and thought about the consequences of this dramatic transformation in anything more than economic terms, let alone spoken out about them in public.
In recent years Havel has expressed satisfaction that the nation is once again respected internationally and on course to join eventually the NATO defence alliance and the European Union.
But he has attacked corruption and the tendency of Czech politicians to put self-interest before the national interest.

"All of us hear around us the alarming extent of corruption, which unfortunately is not proved in many cases, all of us follow with concern news about tax evasion and various kinds of property and financial speculation," he said.

His views seem to have struck a chord with ordinary Czechs. His approval rating is around 80 percent whereas an opinion poll published last week showed that 58 percent of respondents were dissatisfied with the state of Czech politics.
Since Havel became Czechoslovak president in December 1989, a genteel post-communist national consensus has vanished.
Havel resigned in late 1992 rather than preside over the division of Czechoslovakia, negotiated by Czech Prime Minister Klaus with his Slovak counterpart Vladimir Meciar.
He was re-elected president of the Czech Republic alone in early 1993 but in recent years he has been forced to intervene repeatedly to calm an increasingly fractious political scene.

After inconclusive lower house elections, he brokered a power-sharing deal in June this year under which Klaus remained at the head of a minority government while the opposition Social Democrats gained a strong influence in parliament.
But the squabbling intensified during campaigning for Senate elections last month when Klaus and Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman called each other liars.
In the end only 35 percent of voters turned out in the first round and 30 percent in the second. Yet only Havel seemed concerned about what this meant for Czech democracy.
Klaus, who leads the centre-right Civic Democratic Party (ODS), illustrated the difference between Havel who sits above the political fray and the party leaders who are involved in it daily.
"I'm saying here publicly that my aim is not the maximum number of votes. My aim is the maximum number of votes for the ODS," said Klaus, challenging his rivals to admit they thought the same way.
